# How to Use Copilot in Word to Turn a Long Report Into a One-Page Summary

> **In short:** With **Copilot** (Microsoft's AI helper built into Word) you can ask Word to read your long report and produce a short, executive-ready summary in about a minute. You'll need a Microsoft 365 plan that includes Copilot, your report already open in Word, and a clear idea of who will read the summary.

You wrote a 12-page report. Your boss has two minutes. The good news: you don't have to rewrite the whole thing by hand. Copilot lives right inside Word, and one of its most useful tricks is summarizing a long document into something tight. The trick is asking it the right way, and giving the output a quick human polish before you send it.

This guide walks you through the whole thing, step by step, even if you've never opened Copilot before.

## Before you start

- **A Microsoft 365 plan that includes Copilot.** Copilot is a paid add-on, so check that your plan (or your company's plan) actually has it turned on. If you only see "Try Copilot" or no Copilot button at all, the feature isn't on your account yet.
- **The desktop or web version of Microsoft Word** (Windows, Mac, or Word for the web). The exact steps below describe the desktop ribbon, but the web version works almost the same way.
- **Your long report open in Word**, saved as a `.docx` file. It can be a report you wrote, or one a teammate shared with you (as long as you have permission to edit it).
- **Roughly 10–15 minutes**, including time to polish what Copilot gives you.
- A rough sense of **who will read the summary** (your boss? a client? the whole team?) — that one detail makes a big difference in how you phrase your request.

**One honest note:** Copilot is great at cutting length and pulling out key points, but it can sometimes drop a number, miss a nuance, or smooth over a caveat you cared about. Plan to read the summary once before sending it anywhere.

## Step 1 — Open your long report and find the Copilot button

Start by opening the document you want to summarize in Microsoft Word. Now look at the top of the window — that long strip of buttons is called the **ribbon** (think of it as Word's main menu bar). On the **Home** tab, look toward the top-right area for a button labeled **Copilot**. It usually has a small sparkle or ribbon-like icon next to it.

When you click it, a **Copilot chat panel slides open** on the right side of the screen. Your document stays where it is on the left. If you don't see a Copilot button on the Home tab, click the **Home** tab first to make sure you're in the right place, or look for it under a **⋯ (More) menu** or a tab called something like **Copilot** or **Help**.

💬 Example: open `Q3-Project-Update.docx` from your Documents folder and click the **Copilot** button on the Home tab.

You'll know it worked when the chat panel appears on the right and you can see your document still on the left, with a text box at the bottom of the panel where you can type.

## Step 2 — Ask Copilot to summarize the report

In the text box at the bottom of the Copilot panel, type a short request asking for a summary. The clearer you are about **how long** you want it and **who it's for**, the better the result. Copilot works best when you treat it like a quick conversation, not a search engine.

After you press Enter, Copilot reads through your report (this can take 10–30 seconds for a long document) and writes a draft summary directly in the chat panel. It does **not** delete or change your original report — your long version is still safe on the left.

💬 Example: *"Summarize this report into a one-page executive summary. Keep the original tone, the key numbers, and any important dates. Write it for a senior manager who has two minutes to read it."*

You'll know it worked when a block of summary text appears in the Copilot panel, usually with bullet points or short paragraphs, and a small note saying it was generated from your document.

## Step 3 — Tell Copilot how long and what to keep

Your first draft is rarely the final version, and that's normal. Read the draft in the Copilot panel and notice what's missing or off. Then reply in the same chat box with a follow-up request that tightens it up. Common follow-ups: make it shorter, keep only the numbers, write it as one paragraph, or drop the jargon.

Copilot remembers the conversation in the same panel, so each new message refines the previous draft instead of starting over. This is where you save yourself a real round of editing.

💬 Example: *"Shorter. Cut it to about 350 words, keep all the percentages and dollar figures, and remove any section about background context. Use short bullet points under three headings: Wins, Risks, Next Steps."*

You'll know it worked when a new, shorter version replaces the previous one in the panel and you can see the changes are focused on what you asked for (length, format, or specific content).

## Step 4 — Insert the summary into a new document

Once the draft in the panel looks right, you have two choices: insert it straight into the current document, or send it to a new file. For a clean one-pager you'll probably want a **new document** so the original report stays untouched.

Look just below the draft in the Copilot panel for a button that says something like **Insert**, **Add to document**, or **Copy**. If you see an option that says **"Create a new document"** or **"Open in new doc"**, use that — it gives you a blank page with your summary already laid out. If you only see **Insert**, clicking it will paste the summary at your cursor's location in the current document instead, which you can then copy into a new file later.

💬 Example: click **"Create a new document"** (or, if you don't see that exact option, click **Insert**, then press `Ctrl+C` and paste into a fresh blank document).

You'll know it worked when a new Word file opens containing the summary, formatted with the headings and bullet points you asked for, and your original long report is still untouched in its own tab.

## Step 5 — Polish the summary by hand (the part Copilot can't do)

This step is short but important. Read the new one-pager from top to bottom, slowly, as if you were your boss. Cross-check every number, name, and date against the original report on the left. Copilot is good, but it's not perfect — a single wrong percentage is the kind of thing that erodes trust fast.

Tighten anything that sounds generic, fix any sentence that doesn't sound like you, and add a one-line intro or closing if the summary feels abrupt. Usually this takes 2–3 minutes and is what turns a "decent AI draft" into a "boss-ready" one.

💬 Example: if Copilot wrote *"Revenue grew significantly,"* you change it to *"Revenue grew 18% to $4.2M, ahead of the 12% target."*

You'll know it worked when the one-pager reads like something you wrote on a calm Tuesday morning, every number checks out, and the whole thing fits comfortably on a single page.

## Step 6 — Save and share the one-pager

When you're happy with it, save the new file with a clear name so you (and your boss) can find it later. Then share it however your team normally shares documents — email, a chat link, or a shared drive. If you started from someone else's report, you now have **your own separate one-pager**, so you can share just the summary without giving away the full document.

💬 Example: click **File → Save As**, name the file `Q3-Project-Update-OnePager.docx`, and email it to your boss with the subject line *"Q3 update — 2-minute read."*

You'll know it worked when the file is saved, the original long report is still untouched, and the one-pager is ready to send or present.

## Common mistakes

- **Asking for a "summary" with no other details.** If you just type "summarize this," you'll get a generic, sometimes rambling result. Always add the **length** you want (one page, 300 words), the **audience** (my boss, a client, a non-technical reader), and any **must-keep items** (numbers, dates, names).
- **Trusting the first draft without checking.** Copilot can drop, round, or slightly misstate numbers. Always spend two minutes comparing the one-pager against the original report before you send it.
- **Inserting the summary over the original report.** If you use **Insert** instead of **Create a new document**, the summary lands inside your long file. That's fixable (press `Ctrl+Z` to undo), but it's a common beginner slip. When in doubt, copy the summary, open a blank document, and paste it there.

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life:** any time you have a long document (a school paper, a long article, a personal project plan) you can ask Copilot to do the same thing — pull out the key points so you can read the short version first, then dive into the long version only if you need to.
- **For your business or work:** this is one of the fastest ways to produce the executive summary that almost every long report needs. A 12-page status update becomes a one-pager in roughly five minutes of effort, and the rest of the time is polish, not writing.
- **If you're just getting started:** the easiest first move is to pick a report you already have open, run Step 1 and Step 2 exactly as written, and see what comes back. Even a rough first draft tells you a lot about how Copilot handles your kind of writing.

## Try it now

Open any document you have on your screen right now — even a two-page one — click the **Copilot** button in Word, and type: *"Summarize this in five bullet points for a manager who has one minute to read it."* That single 30-second experiment will teach you more about how Copilot works than any article.
